what: AutoNation sells cars. It is one of the largest car dealership groups in the United States, selling new and used vehicles across dozens of brands, servicing and repairing them, selling parts, and arranging finance and insurance on the vehicles it sells.
customers: American car buyers, both new and used, and the same customers returning for servicing and repairs over the vehicle’s life.
money: New car sales, the largest revenue line and the thinnest margin.
Used car sales, where pricing is set by the dealer rather than the manufacturer.
Servicing, repairs and parts, by far the highest-margin business.
Commissions on loans and insurance products sold alongside vehicles.
moat: Franchise agreements with manufacturers are protected by state law in most of the United States, which means a dealership’s right to sell a brand in its area cannot simply be taken away or duplicated. The service business is the real asset: warranty and repair work on vehicles already sold is recurring, high-margin and largely independent of whether anybody is buying new cars.
risks: Free cash flow was only $22.9M against $721.9M of net income, because dealership cash flow is dominated by vehicle inventory financing, which makes the headline figure nearly unusable.
Debt of $4.3B against $58.6M of cash is very heavy, though much of it is floor plan financing secured against vehicles in stock.
A net margin of 2.4% on $27.4B of revenue means there is almost no cushion if vehicle gross profits fall.
New vehicle margins expanded enormously during the supply shortage and have been normalising ever since, which is a headwind that continues.
Electric vehicles need less servicing, which threatens the most profitable part of the business over time.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 8.5 times earnings, 6.6 times EV/EBITDA and 0.21 times sales.
Parts and service is roughly 15% of revenue and a far larger share of profit, and it is tied to the installed base of vehicles rather than to new sales.
Revenue has been stable at $26B to $27.6B through a period of significant disruption in the car market.
Franchise protections in state law make dealership rights genuinely scarce assets.
Twelve analysts average a $213.67 target, about 21% above the current price.
watch: Gross profit per vehicle retailed, and parts and service revenue separately. Revenue in car retailing is almost meaningless; the profit on each car and the service business are the whole story.
view: Car dealerships are routinely misunderstood because the revenue line dominates the page. AutoNation reports $27.4 billion of revenue and earns a 2.4% net margin, which tells you almost all of that figure is the cost of the vehicles passing through. Nobody should value this on revenue, and nobody should value it on the cash flow statement either: free cash flow of $22.9 million against $722 million of net income is a product of vehicle inventory financing, not of the business’s earning power.

What should be valued is gross profit per vehicle and the service business. The profit on each car sold is the variable that swings the earnings, and it expanded enormously during the vehicle shortage when dealers could charge whatever they liked. That has been normalising ever since, and the normalisation is not finished. Anyone extrapolating the last few years of dealership profitability is extrapolating a shortage.

The service business is the part worth owning. Parts and service is about 15% of revenue and a far larger share of profit, and it depends on the vehicles already on the road rather than on anyone buying new ones. Warranty work has to be done at a franchised dealer, the margins are good, and the revenue arrives whether or not the showroom is busy. Combined with franchise protections written into state law — which make the right to sell a brand in a given area a genuinely scarce asset — this is a better business than its margin suggests.

At 8.5 times earnings and 6.6 times EV/EBITDA, you are being paid a low multiple to accept normalising vehicle margins and $4.3 billion of debt. The long-term question that gets too little attention is electrification: an electric vehicle needs substantially less servicing than a combustion one, which over a decade erodes exactly the profit pool that makes dealerships attractive. That is slow and certain rather than sudden, and it is the reason I would treat this as a cheap cyclical rather than a compounder, judged on gross profit per vehicle and service revenue.
bull: Vehicle gross profits stabilise above pre-shortage levels while high-margin service revenue grows on an ageing fleet, and buybacks compound a 8.5 times earnings multiple.
bear: New vehicle margins keep normalising with no cushion at a 2.4% net margin, and electrification steadily erodes the service profit pool that justifies owning dealerships.
